newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea announces record trade deficit for 1996.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea announces record trade deficit for 1996.

text.p: South Korea on Friday posted a record annual trade deficit of $20.38 billion for 1996, chiefly the result of plunging prices for computer chips, but economists said the picture should improve later this year.
The government, meanwhile, said the battle against the ballooning deficit would be the top priority this year along with the fight against inflation.
"Our economic policies will focus on reduction of the current account deficit and price stability," said Finance and Economy Minister Han Seung-soo in a statement.
Trade Ministry figures released on Friday showed December's customs-cleared deficit soared by almost 200 percent to $1.37 billion from $49 million a year ago.
That helped double the full year shortfall to $20.38 billion from $10.06 billion last year.
Pushed by the trade deficit, South Korea's current account shortfall is officially forecast to hit $22 billion in calendar 1996 against an $8.95 billion deficit in 1995.
The current account measures trade in goods and services and certain financial transfers.
The ministry also blamed rising imports of crude oil, the result of a huge expansion by refiners, and a growing taste for luxury imports by South Koreans for the dismal figures.
Officials have declined to forecast this year's trade deficit, but analysts said a slowdown in falling chip prices and a stronger yen should help exporters.
"I see the nation's exports recovering, if slowly, from the second half of this year," said Ohn Ki-un, senior fellow at the government-backed Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade.
"At least a further sharp fall in chip prices is not expected and the yen's value is seen rebounding later this year. These two will be a big help to exporters," Ohn said.
South Korean goods compete in similar markets with Japanese products, which have been boosted by a weaker yen.
Ohn said the yen was expected to reach its bottom of between 115 and 120 yen per dollar during the second quarter of this year before rebounding.
The Korea Institute has forecast this year's customs-cleared trade deficit at $17.5 billion, while the central Bank of Korea has put it at around $15.5 billion.
Total exports rose 3.8 percent to $129.83 billion in 1996, dragged down by a 19.2 percent fall in the value of semiconductor sales to $17.87 billion.

"Excluding semiconductors, our exports grew by 8.8 percent in 1995, outpacing the ministry's earlier target of an 8.1 percent rise," Kim Sang-yeol, chief of the ministry's trade policy department, told reporters.
Kim said world prices of the most widely-used 16-megabit Dynamic Random Access Memory chips had fallen 81.7 percent to $9.25 per unit at the end of 1996 from $50.6 a year earlier.
Imports gained 11.2 percent to $150.21 billion in 1996, but consumer product imports surged by 20.6 percent.
"Rises in grains prices and a rush of luxury consumer good imports as a result of increased income has combined to push up imports," Kim said.
Along with rises in international crude prices, capacity expansion by major refining firms led to a sharp 31.8 percent rise in crude imports in 1996, Kim said.
